utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday, 10th of December, 2008. Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, can we move to private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us wait until the blinds are up. Sir, please state your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovan Glamocanin, born on the 16th of June, 1940, in Subotica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a retiree, but I have a degree in law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had an opportunity to testify before a domestic or international court of law as to the events in the former Yugoslavia or is this going to be the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I'm testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we start asking questions of you and providing you with information, I believe Mr. Seselj had a request. Did you have anything to say, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let me explain to you several things. You have been called to testify by the Trial Chamber, therefore at the request of the Judges of the Bench in front of you. I recall or remind you of some facts, and I know you're a lawyer; and I'm sure, therefore, that you will understand straight away what I'm about to say. It is true that you had not requested any protective measures back then, but on the 15th of February, 2005, the OTP had made an application to another Trial Chamber than this one for protective measures, and in the filings made by the OTP, it was alleged that you had some fear for pressure or harassment. That's the reason why protective measures had been granted to you. A pseudonym had also been given, "VS-044." Later on, you told the OTP that you didn't need any protective measures. The OTP had taken you out of their 65 ter witness list in 2007 because, from the point of view of the procedure, the indictment against Mr. Seselj had been reduced, and therefore there were witnesses that were no longer needed. That's the reason why you were struck off their list. Later on, the OTP made another application for your name to be added to the witness list, and on the 17th of June, 2008, the Trial Chamber had granted the application. Why were protective measures applied for? We'll get to that later on, but it's also because in your statement you had said that at some point in time, people close to the Serb Radical Party allegedly tried to kidnap your wife or your daughter - we're not quite sure about that - and that you had hired bodyguards, and that was the setting in which the protective measures had been granted. And then a series of events took place. You had some fear. You feared being assassinated, and you no longer wished to testify. There was quite some spectacular event that took place; namely, that publicly you stated that you were going to be a Defence witness, that is, a witness for Mr. Seselj; and together with Mr. Vujic, on the 20th of November, 2007, you took part in a press conference during which you publicly stated that you were going to be a Defence witness. You even granted an interview after that to 'Pravda,' and you blamed the Prosecution or accused the Prosecution, but I'm not going to go into that. So the Judges were faced with an unheard-of problem so far in the history of the Tribunal, namely, that a Prosecution witness was then saying that he was going to be a Defence witness, and we had to sort it out. We were of the view that we were able to find a solution by calling you as a witness, by issuing a summons for you to come and testify. You were then called by a judge in Belgrade, who conveyed this to you. On the 4th of November, 2008, you sent me a mail in which you explained that you were a Defence witness, inasmuch as you felt that the statement you had made over four days in 2003 was not Prosecution evidence against Mr. Seselj, in your view, and that you wanted to be a Defence witness, as you were of the view that Mr. Seselj was innocent, not guilty of the charges against him. This being so, we maintained the summons. This is the reason why you appear here today, and just as well, because if you had failed to appear, we would have been forced to indict you for contempt of court, and this would have sent you straight away to jail. So you were right in meeting our summons. The purpose is this: We want to have the truth manifested, to know exactly what happened in that period of the years 1992 and 1993. We want to know what the involvement of the SRS was in certain events, what everybody's part was. We want to know what your position was within the SRS. These are questions that can be answered through your presence in a very serene and calm manner, so that this hearing can unfold as smoothly as possible. By way of explanation, I also add that the Judges -- I'll start, but that the Judges have a series of questions for you. It should take one and a half to two hours. Thereafter, the parties, that is, the Prosecution and Mr. Seselj, will each have an hour to put questions to you, questions that they deem appropriate. Have you understood everything I said? You're aware of the climate and spirit in which you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are, first of all, interested in knowing your professional background, your education in particular. Could you, in a few words, tell us what your university background is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: First of all, I studied at the Higher School for State Administration. Then I went to the Law Faculty, and I held high positions in the business community and in the state administration. I was secretary of two companies: One was an agricultural farm and the other one was a construction company. I was general manager of a big factory, the Utva aircraft factory. I was a member of the board in charge of general and legal matters, and of course I was a federal MP too. After leaving the Serb Radical Party, I became rather passive, politically speaking, but so far I've completed about ten serious papers, namely, seven papers and eight books pertaining to the state system, the political system. I'm preoccupied with the fate of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we could not hear the witness due to background noise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have been dealing with the -- rather, I have been dealing with the history of the Serbian people, and I became, therefore, a member of the Academy of Spiritual Work. It is -- its seat is in Crimea, in Russia, but then it is also in other countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall return to several of these points, but let's focus on your university background. You studied at the law school in the Belgrade University. I guess that you graduated, you got a license, or a BA, or a doctorate. What is the exact title?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: No. On the basis of these papers and books I've written, I became a member of this academy, a regular member. It's not a state academy. It was established by creative people from different walks of life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. There must have been a hitch in the translation. I was asking you this: You studied at the university, and I wanted to know whether, when you were studying at the law school, you eventually graduated, and you graduated with a PhD in law, or a Master's, or a BA; what is the actual degree that you got?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I got my law degree in Belgrade. I have a diploma, a BA as a jurist. As for these other scholarly works that I engaged in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could no longer hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not interested in the books, but you said that you are -- you graduated in law. What was your specialty in law, because I noticed that you wrote papers --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: The stream that I studied at was commercial law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In commercial law, I see.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Matters pertaining to procedural law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to your career, your professional background, you said that you had various occupations, you worked in many companies.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I was secretary of the municipality, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but let's wait until we get to the political side of things. I'm still with the administrative matters. In the various posts that you occupied, I think that the common denominator was that they basically focused on administrative matters, logistical and organisational matters. Was that your primary skill, when it came to those positions?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I also worked in the business community. I was a member of the collective general manager, as it were. I was a member of a board of a big company, big in terms of our country, on that scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now deal with the political part. I was under the impression that after doing your military service in the JNA, just like any other citizen, you then, in 1963, joined the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: That is correct. I joined the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. I was a member of the municipal committee and the district committee of the League of Youth of Subotica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Were you then a firm believer of communism or did you join the League of Communists because it was the only way to get anywhere in high positions?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you know what, at that time lawyers didn't have much of a choice. They had to be involved in the existing political and economic system. That was one of the motives. The second motive was that this self-management socialist Yugoslavia was a progressive, respectable state, and I think that through one's knowledge and one's work, one was supposed to help the development of that country. It was a successful country, from the point of view of the economy, from the point of view of foreign policy, in every conceivable point of view. Over here, even, in this court, it was often pointed out that we had a very good and capable army, and in all other fields we were a country that prospered. I believed, as a citizen, that it was my responsibility to give a contribution that even exceeded what my obligation might have been. I liked that country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. So in order to contribute to the country that you say you loved, you took up positions at municipal level. What prompted you to enter that sphere of municipal politics.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, in my career I was never in a position to make requests, to ask for something. Every time when I would change jobs, people asked me to move on, to take a job that was even more complex, because up until then I had been successful in carrying out my duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the reason why you joined the municipal administration?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us now speak about your political involvement before you joined the Serb Radical Party. Could you, in a few words, tell me what you did politically, knowing that the League of Communists is an organisation that you're going to leave, that you left in order to move on to political actions by way of writing articles, et cetera; so could you say some more about it as to your political involvement before you joined the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was always preoccupied with the fate of my state, especially of my people, the Serb people. In my family, many people had lost their lives in the most recent wars, and in all the wars in which the Serb people had participated and suffered greatly. As secretary of the municipality in Banat from 1974 onwards, that is to say from the moment when this Constitution of Yugoslavia was adopted, namely, the Constitution that transformed Yugoslavia partly into a confederacy, I immediately came to the conclusion that that kind of a community, that kind of a setup, was incapable of functioning properly. Nevertheless, Yugoslavia did function. However, what I found interesting and what I thought was unacceptable was the fact that Serbia was subdivided into three parts. It had two provinces that were completely independent and geared towards the federation, in terms of all its powers. Vis a vis Serbia, it only had a formal relationship, proof to tell, the Constitution did provide -- the Constitution of Yugoslavia and the Constitution of Serbia, that is, did provide for the possibility of transferring some authority to Serbia itself that basically was given to the provinces by the Constitution. However, this was not taken advantage of. On the contrary, separatists and independents grew in both provinces. As for Vojvodina, there were no inter-ethnic tensions, none that I would have noticed, but in Kosmet there were major problems. These problems escalated at the time of the crisis faced by Yugoslavia, and as a person who is primarily engaged in patriotism rather than politics, I joined this movement to save the Serb people in Kosovo and Metohija and to have Kosmet and Vojvodina returned within the state structure of the Republic of Serbia. Since that was my option, from an emotional and a rational point of view, vis a vis our people, the Serb people, and the other peoples -- of course, I'm not in favour of any kind of mistreatment, or any kind of force, or any kind of discrimination against any people, may I add; however, I joined a movement that we then called the Serb People's Movement, or, rather, the People's Movement for a United Serbia. And later on, I was one of the top people of that movement for Vojvodina, and it was on the crest of that movement that Kosovo and Metohija and Vojvodina were returned in 1989 to the state structure of Serbia, because the Constitution of Serbia was amended. As an individual, as an intellectual, I took part in that movement. I made my proposals in newspapers. I was the first one in Vojvodina to do so, in order to have these amendments passed to the Constitution of Serbia, these amendments that restored the authority of Serbia over both provinces. Later on, I wrote a study, a paper, about autonomy. Later on, I expanded it and wrote a book. I think that many scholars, including a lady who testified here, Smilja Avramov, believe this is the best book written in the territory of the former Yugoslavia about the subject matter of autonomy. I was in this movement. I was arrested four times by the State Security Service, but of course I persevered because I was convinced that I was fighting for the right thing, for elementary rights; the right to life, the right to freedom of the Serbian people and all citizens of Serbia and Yugoslavia. And this did not lead me to waver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you, sir, because your answer returns over several pages of the transcript, and this is a complex matter and I have to sum it up. Your approach seems to be connected to the following observation you made: You realised that Vojvodina and Kosovo-Metohija were, in relation to Serbia, autonomous or quasi-autonomous areas, and your fight was to try and unify all this within the Republic of Serbia. Based on that, you wrote papers and you tried to make yourself known. This political fight, the struggle you fought, was basically focused, as I understood you, on the situation in Kosovo-Metohija, and this resulted in you having some political weight in Serbia. Is this the way we can sum up what you did before you met with the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to make things clear, clarify one of your questions. I didn't fight against the autonomy of Vojvodina, Kosmet, within the frameworks of Serbia, but I fought against the status of both Vojvodina and Kosmet in which they were completely autonomous and independent in relation to Serbia, because the provinces had their constitution, they had their police force, they had their legal organs, courts. Serbia only had formal authority over the provinces. And in addition to that, I also fought to have a realistic status given to the provinces, because that was one of the conditions for Yugoslavia, as a state, to be able to function. So in that struggle of mine, I and all those who took part in this did not question Yugoslavia and the functioning of Yugoslavia. I became well known. I was at the head of the organisation which was called the Alliance of Solidarity of Yugoslavia or Union of Solidarity, and the Serbian Radical Party had not been established at that time. I became a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. And in this court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, before we get to the Serbian Chetnik Movement. I would like us to stay in 1990. It seems that in 1990, you will set up a small party. Could you tell us exactly which party you set up.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: The party was not well known. It was just a contribution to try to force the powers that be to allow us to set up new political parties or, rather, to introduce a multiparty system. And it was on the basis of that popular movement for a united Serbia, which the regime of Slobodan Milosevic had to accept, was forced to accept, we had discussions with Slobodan Milosevic which lasted six and a half hours, and our activists from Kosmet and Vojvodina were there. And at the meeting, we managed to convince him that a multiparty system must be introduced in Serbia. And it's interesting to note that at that meeting, it was concluded that new parties should not be established, that we should not form new parties. But we persevered and did stand by our decision to set up a party, and it's interesting that the conclusion of the session was that parties should not be formed, but we nevertheless went ahead and did form a party. And a week later, there was a proclamation after the meeting, a statement after it, when they saw that we had set our minds to form the parties and persevere that the citizens of Serbia should be allowed to establish parties. So that was our role. We put in a lot of effort there, and the State Security did its best to suppress us and our actions, but we never spared any effort because we managed to achieve one of our goals, and that was to introduce democracy into Serbia and a multiparty parliamentary democracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I'm not mistaken, this was called the Democratic Party of Freedom in your own language, "Demokratska Stranka Slobode," and I apologise for my pronunciation. Was that what this party was called?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, that's what it was called, the "Demokratska Stranka Slobode."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this is an interesting contribution, because so far this had not been mentioned. So you were talking to Mr. Milosevic, and you tried to get him to understand that he had to move the country into a multiparty democracy. And it's in this framework that you set up your small party, but obviously he didn't really like the idea. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: I was in favour of having Serbia take on the initiative in restructuring the state in this transition towards a democratic system, and that we should have the initiative -- take the initiative within Yugoslavia, because there was a crisis looming in Yugoslavia. The Croats and Slovenians had taken this initiative, and they got the advantage, which they used with respect to Germany, the Vatican, later on the United States and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why didn't you join the Socialist Party of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I didn't join the Socialist Party of Serbia because it was a party which was formed in an inconsistent way. The League of Communists of the day and the Socialist Alliance of the Working People of Yugoslavia transformed itself to become the Socialist Party. Now, I respect people with conviction, who act in politics on the basis of their convictions and on the basis of their ideology, and not on the basis of the wish to rule and to take advantages of the existing situation, opportunistically, and that's what happened. It happened in all countries of transition. The former Communist parties became Socialist parties. I was in favour of democracy. Those were my beliefs. I come from a family that has those traditions. My father fought for democracy, and he emerged from World War II as a Chetnik commander. And here Chetniks are spoken about in a derogatory manner. There's a derogatory view of them, unfavorable, but I'll explain that in due course later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's come closer to the very heart of the matter, which is your joining the Serbian Radical Party. Could you please tell us whether at the time, February/March 1991, tell us what you -- what was your impression of the Serbian Radical Party at the time, as well as of its leader, Mr. Seselj? What was the impact of this party and its leader on the political life at the time, and on what grounds did you decide to join this party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I first met Mr. Seselj as the president of the Serbian Freedom-Loving Movement, which was the first political organisation which he established, and that was a political party with a Yugoslav orientation. And I remember well that one of my co-fighters from Bosnia, Asim Delic, for example, was one of the founding members of that Serbian Freedom-Loving Movement. It was a movement of distinct Yugoslav orientation. Asim Delic fought in Bosnia against the bureaucracy that had entrenched itself there and sought greater freedoms for the citizens. They had Galijasevic with them and many others. And if I can put it this way, the prime political fighters for the new democratic system and the reconstruction of Yugoslav based on democracy went along with Dr. Seselj; and they promoted a programme and policy for the defence of Serb national interests, but within the frameworks of Yugoslavia, of the Yugoslav community. And Dr. Vojislav Seselj remained along those lines up until the formation of the Chetnik Movement and the Serbian Radical Party. He remained true to those ideals of adopted the same position. Of course, when Yugoslavia disintegrated and fell apart, and when foreign forces -- foreign intelligence services became involved and meddled, and they destroyed that joint state, we had to think about the fate of our own people, our own nation, and seek out a programme by which we would be able to defend the interests and protect the interests of our people, because on the political arena of Yugoslavia or, rather, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Kosmet, we had the burgeoning of destructive forces that came to the fore, which in World War II were on the side of Hitler's Germany, and Mussolini, and they effected genocide over the Serbian and other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have told us at length what Mr. Seselj might have embodied, but I believe that I understood that you did not join because of Mr. Seselj because of a number of ideas that could have allowed the Yugoslav people, in all its diversity, to face up to the collapse of the country. So could you tell us, in details, exactly what, in 1990 and 1991, were the values that the Serbian people wanted to obtain and reach? What could have been the political platform of a party bringing together a number of people that could promote a project? Could you tell us what the objective of such a political party could be?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: The objectives were the preservation of Yugoslavia as a stable, multinational community, without bringing into question the interests of each and every one of the Yugoslav peoples, the national minorities too, and also to establish a position of equality for the Serbian people, because it was quite obvious that the Serb people were being expelled from Kosovo and Metohija. There were many cases of violence against the Serb people, and you have the following piece of information, for example. In the 1939 census, Serbs and Siptars or, rather, Albanians, there was an equal number; 10.000 or 15.000 less Serbs. Now, according to the census -- well, it wasn't in 1991. But, anyway, according to the next census, the Serbs dropped to 200.000, to the figure of 200.000 -- or, rather, 300.000. Now, today, there are just about 150.000 Serbs in Kosmet, or even less. So it wasn't the number of Siptars that decreased in Kosovo and Metohija, with all the authority that Yugoslavia and Serbia had, but it was the number of Serbs that were reduced. The Siptars had their own movement of independence geared towards a Greater Albania. It wasn't a movement that was created while the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in existence. It was formed much earlier than that. I don't want to go into the history of the Serb people and all the suffering from Albanian terrorism, but it was all -- the Turkish empire, under the Turkish empire for 500 years, Hitler's state, Mussolini's state. During the communist state, it was always the Serbs that suffered, and now we have the domination of the United States of America. So it's we Serbs who fall casualty and suffer every time, and of course we had to seek a way to resist this or, rather, to return part of the state functions of Serbia and of Yugoslavia to -- to bring it back to the area of Kosovo and Metohija. When in 1981 the Presidency of Yugoslavia decided to bring in the police from all the Yugoslav republics to Kosovo, we Serbs weren't opposed to that because we didn't see that we were violating any sovereign rights because we were in favour of Yugoslavia and the Yugoslav Federation. And now this movement for a united Serbia, it was a truly Yugoslav movement, and I joined Mr. Seselj as the president of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, because the Serbian Chetnik Movement, in its party programme, had the -- had to preserve Yugoslavia, to preserve the parliamentary system, multiparty parliamentary system, democracy and capitalism, on the foundations of the programme of Draza Mihajlovic, the Chetnik commander from World War II. And as far as Draza Mihajlovic is concerned, much has been said about him, things that are not true. He was a very well-educated officer. He graduated from the academy, military academy, with Charles de Gaulle. He graduated from the military academy in Paris, and his programme was almost identical to the resistance movement of Charles de Gaulle. And as I say, Draza was a democratic. However, the unfortunate thing was that we had two movements in World War II. And the other unfortunate thing was that in our Yugoslav Federation, there was always foreign interference in a destructive way, so the centres of those powers were in Germany and in the Vatican, that's where they were to be had. And I think that Dr. Seselj is the person who studied all this in depth and comprehensively. So it was from those positions that I joined the Serbian Chetnik Movement, whose president was Dr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You gave us the reason why you joined this movement led by Mr. Seselj. Now, from what you just told us, I would like to highlight two things. First, the situation in Kosovo-Metohija. Obviously, for a Serb, it's a real problem. According to the figures you just gave us, you felt that the number of Serbs in this area was decreasing, and this was a critical problem, nationally. The second problem you seem to highlight and which motivated your joining the Chetnik Movement is that according to you, there were some intervention from foreigners. You mentioned two more -- you mentioned two foreign influences, Germany and the Vatican. And then you tell us that all this was mentioned in Mr. Seselj's books. Then you joined the Chetnik Movement. Can you tell us what this movement represented at the time within the Serb community? What did it represent, in terms of man count, and what was its political influence, what was its weight? What was the importance of the Serbian Chetnik Movement at the time, when we know that we also had Milosevic and the Socialist Party, his Socialist Party? Tell us about the importance of the Chetnik Movement in the political scene at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, that movement meant a great deal in the moral sense. It awakened feelings of Serb solidarity. It awakened people to the truth. It showed us that we had to look at the situation realistically. It pointed out the dangers that threatened the joint state and showed the dangers that threatened the Serb people. It wasn't the goal of the Chetnik Movement to create a clash with Milosevic, but we were convinced that Milosevic, too, was in favour of preserving Yugoslavia, but at the same time we knew that Milosevic wanted to stay in power and to transform his power in the extent and manner to which -- which would ensure his positions in future. So we did not want to have any conflicts or clashes, we did not want to break up Yugoslavia; quite the contrary. It was our aim to preserve Yugoslavia, but we wanted to awaken the nation's consciousness and to ensure that the Serb people looked at the situation realistically, and also to awaken their readiness for the defence of Yugoslavia and the Serb people. Now, let me tell you this: The traditions of the Chetnik Movement are, in fact, the traditions of the Serb people, and those traditions emerge from the times of Kosovo, and loyalty to the Chetnik Movement means that you are ready to lay down your -- to give up -- lay down your lives for Serbia and Serb rights, and we had to be ready to defend our religion too, because it was under threat with the advent of the Turks, and today, too. For example, in Montenegro, there's a new religion being imposed upon us, and there's no realistic basis for that, either moral, or religious, or doctrinaire, or any other for some new religion. So that were our aim, those were our objectives. And the longstanding tradition of the Chetnik Movement was to fight like a knight, honourably, and when read all the Serb poems and look back to Serb poetry, you can see how the Serbs envisaged warriors fighting for freedom. And also this includes nurturing humane qualities and noble qualities in going into battle; that is to say that you must kill the frail, you must not kill civilians, you must not kill people you have captured. The struggle against people who are out to kill you and kill your people and nation, and people who are out to kill and abuse people in general, that was who we were fighting against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it so happens that we had a number of witnesses in this Tribunal, not intellectuals -- I'm not talking about intellectuals, but people who had an average level of education, and they did come and tell us and explain why they joined the Chetnik Movement or the Serbian Radical Party. And these people, who did not have the excellent education that you had or the high-profile positions that you had, told us that they joined this movement for reasons that had to do with monarchy, because they wanted the king to come back, they wanted monarchy to be re-installed. We heard this a number of times. So what do you -- could you tell us what you think of this monarchist trend within the Chetnik Movement, because we have a number of witnesses who told us that that was the reason they joined. And to tell you the truth, we almost feel that they haven't really understood what was the final objective sought by the party, because they just wanted the king to come back. They wanted to have a king on a throne in Yugoslavia. So what do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, this is what I think; that the king was more a symbol of changing the social system, that is to say, leaving behind communism and introducing a multiparty democracy and everything else that a new society would bring with it. But let me tell you, Aleksandar Karadjordjevic, when he arrived in Serbia, the heir to the throne, he lost all belief that the monarchy was the real solution. Well, he didn't learn his mother tongue, for instance. It's not nice to say bad things about one's king, but he doesn't appear to be too intelligent, he doesn't seem to have the kind of conduct that European kings have. He even appeared funny in certain situations and did not instill respect and did not show that he could contribute to his nation and his state in any way, so that initial desire that we had to have a king, to have a king who would help us in transforming society, and contribute to saving democracy, well, that bubble burst; and the first person to understand and realised that was Mr. Seselj, and he also had an opportunity of getting to know the heir to the throne more closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems Mr. Seselj was inspired by a person called Nikola Pasic. Can you tell us who this person was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Ah, Nikola Pasic. Nikola Pasic was the greatest Serbian politician of the 20th century. That's who he was, he was a consistent fighter, fought for the interests of his country, his nation, but always in favour of democracy. He was a fervent royalist. He respected king and country, but he had a lot of problems with everyone, with King Milan and with King Aleksandar Obrenovic, and with that other one, Karadjordjevic -- the Karadjordjevics, both Petar and Aleksandar, and he died after having been to an audience with King Aleksandar, at which Aleksandar I, Karadjordjevic, was rude to Nikola Pasic and said -- had some criticisms of his son. But, anyway, Nikola Pasic has left an indelible trace on the country and the Serb people, and especially his beliefs in democracy. He had a fervent belief in democracy, and Nikola Pasic is the most deserving politician, most deserving for all the things that the Serb people achieved in the Balkan wars, in World War I, when we made our contribution beyond and above the size of our country and the strength of our country. And then the Western countries and all the freedom-loving countries acknowledged that and respected him and the country, and our alliance with the French people, for example, and the French state. But unfortunately in this latest war, things have made an about-turn, unfortunately, because the destructive forces in Western Europe and later on in the United States of America did something quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, Nikola Pasic was a politician who was inspiring the idea of democracy. He was a major democrat, a leading democrat, if we had to sum up his personality and his contribution to Mr. Seselj's ideas.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that would be true. Nikola Pasic made the greatest contribution to further the democratic traditions in Serbia, of course, but also for the defence of state and national sovereignty. He wielded the greatest influence on politics. And after the ultimatum that Austria-Hungary made to Serbia, and that ultimatum had the aim of -- it was an ultimatum that Serbia could not accept in July 1914. He accepted all the conditions laid down except for one, and that was that Austro-Hungarian police could enter Serbia to carry out an investigation, and he demonstrated how the sovereignty of the country should be defended by doing that. And now tell me what kind of sovereignty we have in Serbia today, when the US intelligence service and Javier Solana decide who's going to be our minister, who's going to lead our government, what kind of monetary we're going to have, open telephone lines, and so on and so forth? So we believed the West --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are now dealing with the present politician situation, but we're interested in the past. We're interested in the years 1990-1991, and Pasic. We're not going to discuss Mr. Solana at the moment. So let's come back to 1991. You told us about the Serbian Radical Party. You joined it, and if I'm not mistaken, I believe that you were appointed to a senior post within the leading -- within the leaders of the Serbian Radical Party. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, at the founding Assembly of the Serb Radical Party, I was elected member of the Main Board. However, I actively joined the Serb Radical Party activities only in September because I was wrapping up my activities in the People's Movement for a United Serbia. That movement was still functioning up until mid-1991. That is when I was given the office of head of the Regional Board for Banat. That is what the internal setup of the Serb Radical Party was like then, according to regions, with a central organ, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Banat area, how far is it from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: No, Banat is right below Belgrade. Pancevo is the town that I live in, and it's 12 kilometres away from Belgrade. Speaking from a strictly geographic point of view, the area of the city of Belgrade even includes a small part of Banat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's very close to Belgrade. You mentioned Pancevo, and I understood that you organised the first visit made by Mr. Seselj to that town.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj had this public position as head of the Serb Radical Movement, so his voice was heard in the public. I did things within the scope of the time frame allowed by Mr. Seselj's schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were present, as I understand it, when Mr. Seselj made a speech in Pancevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we could not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me how Mr. Seselj, as a politician, made that speech? How was it organised? Did he have prepared speeches or did he improvise as he was going along? Did he manage to establish a close contact with those who attended a political meeting? Was he a real public speaker? Could you, in a few words, tell us how he was as an orator?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: One cannot say that Mr. Seselj improvises. He has a great deal of knowledge, and he plans his public appearances. Mr. Seselj can be inspired by a big gathering of people, but Mr. Seselj never steps out of the framework of his programme and his convictions. He knows how to establish contact. He knows how to work an audience, how to thrill an audience, especially consisting of members of our own people, but also the national minorities. He does not speak about conflicts among people and nations. He does not talk about discrimination. He doesn't talk about persecutions, genocide. He talks about resolving problems. He indicates, in realistic terms, what the situation is like. He does not talk like most politicians, only from the point of view of daily political interests. Rather, he speaks from the point of view of the actual situation as it is, the possible consequences, and he offers solutions. Therefore, Mr. Seselj does not really improvise. Rather, there is inspiration. But Mr. Seselj has a very strong will, and he can control himself and the expression of his thoughts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean that when Mr. Seselj makes a speech - and the reason why I'm asking you this is that Mr. Seselj's speeches are very relevant in this case - so when he makes a speech, does that mean that the speech has already been worked up, I mean, prepared by him or his associates; therefore, when he appears publicly, everything he's going to say has been thought through, prepared, and that there is no room for this last-minute improvisation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you know what -- oh, no, no. What I was trying to say was that Mr. Seselj never goes outside the framework of his principles and convictions, the positions that he holds and the conclusions that he came to through his process of thought. As for preparations, Seselj did not have any associates who could help him in preparing his speeches. Seselj is by far the smartest one, the one with the greatest body of knowledge and the person with a vision in the Serb Radical Party at the time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I understand it, when Mr. Seselj would go to hold speeches, would go to rallies, he would get there, forgive me the expression, with his hands in his pockets, so rested, but he would launch into a speech that would mirror very faithfully his thoughts?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly, his convictions and the programme of the Serb Radical Party. Of course, for the most part, he was the one who wrote the programme. It is the fruit of his ideas and his thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer as to the manifesto, the programme of the Serbian Radical Party, makes it possible for me to now delve into the inner workings of the SRS. From what I understood, between the time when you joined and the time when you left the party on the 7th of October, 1994, you were a vice-president in the party, in charge of organisational matters and personnel. The party also had structures at the level of republics. I mean to say that the SRS, from what I gather from the system, had people in other republics. Is that how I am to understand the way the SRS worked?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Exactly. The Serb Radical Party existed for the Republic of the Serb Krajina and for Republika Srpska and for Montenegro. These parties acted in a united manner. The presidents of these parties and the leaderships of these parties discussed things and reached agreement with Mr. Seselj and the rest of us. We had a joint programme, but each and every one of these parties was registered in their respective states on the basis of the laws of those states. Coordination was serious, but they did act independently in the parliaments of these three other Serb states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me who was the one in charge of the SRS for the Republika Srpska and who was the one responsible for the party in the Krajina? Who were the two individuals heading the SRS in those two areas?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I remember. In Republika Srpska, there was Poplasen, Professor Poplasen. I've forgotten his name. And in the Republic of Serb Krajina, Rade Leskovac, a well-known journalist. And in Montenegro, Acim Visnjic [phoen]. Now, was there anyone else? Radovan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as part of the way the SRS would work, would Mr. Seselj have political working sessions with his close vice-presidents or with the secretary-general? We had the pleasure of meeting and seeing him a while ago. Would he have meetings with other people in charge of the SRS in other republics? Were there high-level meetings with all the players?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: There were meetings, and Mr. Seselj consulted with us, the vice-presidents. He maintained the functioning of all the organs of the party in accordance with the statute. However, there is one thing that is characteristic of the Serb Radical Party; namely, that Mr. Seselj dominated the party, but not on the basis of some kind of threats or some other undemocratic measures. Rather, it was on the basis of his knowledge, on the basis of how well-spoken he was. He works the most, by far. He can make great efforts. He's a visionary, too. We all respected him. Some people do not understand Mr. Seselj because he tends to speak in a loud voice. He sometimes raises his voice, too. However, a man who works that hard and is so involved in the creative process sometimes does get tired, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just confirmed that there were meetings which you necessarily attended. Were there minutes of these meetings or were minutes never taken?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, there were some working meetings before a session, especially when a big rally was supposed to be attended or, say, a meeting at a municipal committee, or some other assignment, then no minutes were needed. We discussed who would go where, who would discuss the economy, who would discuss foreign policy, social policy, and so on and so forth. However, at the Main Board, at the meetings of organs envisioned by the statute, minutes were invariably kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So minutes were always taken, and if these minutes exist, they should be in the archives of the SRS, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: The Main Board, the Executive Board, that's for sure, the Central Fatherland, although I really did not concern myself with minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll get back to that later on. But as to the issue of the volunteers of the SRS, I guess that when the decision was made at SRS level to dispatch volunteers to various fronts, was there a meeting about it? If so, were you there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, when I got actively involved in the work of the Serb Radical Party, that is to say, in the month of September, what I found there was intensive activity in terms of the volunteers going to join JNA units and Territorial Defence units or, rather, organisation for war. Of course, there were discussions at sessions concerning the participation of volunteers. However -- well, you know what, we did not have any kind of war staff; in name, yes, but we didn't have a war staff that had some kind of equipment or that was engaged in some kind of command, or that was in charge of some kind of war affairs, no. I organised the departure of volunteers from the area of Banat, and we did that in the following way: They'd call us from Belgrade, from the War Staff, telling us that the JNA and then later on the army of Republika Srpska or the army of Krajina needed volunteers. Then we would call these volunteers of ours and we'd send them to Belgrade. From there, they went to Bubanj Potok or wherever. What was a specific characteristic in our sending of volunteers was that we would always take our volunteers to the church to take Holy Communion, which was a Serb tradition from the time of the battle of Kosovo. Before the battle started, the soldiers took Holy Communion. And then the priests spoke about the need to defend the Serb people, but that they should wage war in a chivalrous manner and in a noble manner. I was present once or twice when a larger number of volunteers were leaving. That is the same thing that Mr. Seselj said, too. He never said, "We are going to go out there to kill the Croats, be merciless," which would be in the tradition of some of the great European nations. On the contrary, he always said, "No, you have to defend the Serb people, the Serb people have to go on living in these areas, but fight in a chivalrous manner like your forefathers from the days of Kosovo onwards, be noble, do not commit any evil."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, a question comes straight to the mind of an outside observer or a judge. Why, in the defence of the former Yugoslavia, as it then existed, was defence not to be carried out by the JNA, by the people's army? Why not resort to, quote/unquote "volunteers" who would, like knights of the Middle Ages go, once they had taken Holy Communion, why would they not go to combat? Why not choose such individuals, as the very essence of any country, is that armed forces are under the authority of a central state? Why did you encapsulate, encompass, that notion of volunteers? We've already heard a lot about it, but since you're here before us, I have to put the question as well.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. President, Yugoslavia did not collapse within three days. It was a process, after all. In this process, there were many forces at play in a destructive fashion. All of Slovenia was on the move. They wanted to secede unilaterally without appropriate procedure. They even killed our soldiers. They did not allow recruits to go to the Yugoslav People's Army. The same thing happened with Croatia. Even in Serbia, we had destructive activity. We had a Vuk Draskovic, who called upon recruits from Central Serbia, Kragujevac, Valjevo, et cetera, not to join the JNA. Now, these calls, had they been peaceful, would have been reasonable ones. However, out there, they were killing Serb people. There were still these new paramilitary formations. There was the Yugoslavia, though, so the Serb people were in jeopardy. Other people would be in jeopardy, too. So the JNA needed additional assistance from those who wanted to fight. It is on that basis that volunteers from Serbia, believing in the Serb Radical Party, believing in Dr. Seselj, went there through the Serb Radical Party. They could have gone directly through the JNA, too. However, they had this special belief in Dr. Seselj, because he indicated what the times were like and everything that was happening at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You, yourself, said that you personally organised the departure of Serbian volunteers from the Banat area, so you know this area very well. As far as you know, the volunteers who would leave and had been armed by the JNA, because I suppose that you did not provide them with weapons, is that right; so under whose authority or under whose command were they put?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Under the command of the JNA. The Radical Party did not have any formations, any commanders, any commanding officers, any military structure of units, and it didn't have people who knew how to do that kind of thing, nor did it take part in war operations through its people. We only looked at this civilian aspect of the departure of volunteers going into the war. Later on, when volunteers would return, we took care of them, especially those who were wounded or those who got killed. We collected aid, and quite a few managers of different companies helped us. It was easier for me in Pancevo because I was a colleague of the general managers of big companies, and they really tried to do what they could for us. They even gave apartments to the families of fallen soldiers. It was the state that resolved other matters, it was the army that resolved other matters; but, anyway, we worked in helping the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could show you documents regarding the logistics and the assistance you provided to volunteers, but there's no need for that. The documents have been admitted already. I'd rather go to the crux of the matter. As I understand it, the volunteers who would leave, who were under the command of the Territorial Defence or the JNA, nevertheless kept some kind of connection with the Serb Radical Party regarding the situation of the volunteers, be it only if they were wounded, or killed, or had trouble getting money or being paid; can you confirm that? Can you confirm that there was some kind of link or a follow-up of the volunteers at the level of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, we only followed this up from the point of view of this social welfare, this aid, trying to help these people. They were on these lists of volunteers that were made even before the war broke out, and we'd call them to come. Many of them were members of the Serb Radical Party. Some of them were even members of the leadership of the party. But you know what? All of this was done in a situation and an atmosphere conducive to helping one's people, defending lives and property of our own people in the war-engulfed areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you describe how the War Staff worked that was led by Petkovic? Could you tell us who were the members of the War Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, in addition to Mr. Petkovic, I remember Rankic, but they -- they did not seem like any kind of warriors to me, or officers, or something like that. They looked like people who were being engaged, who were working very hard in assisting volunteers to leave and helping their families to the best of one's ability. Well, it was like a service. There was this work in terms of organising departures, and then meeting volunteers when they'd come back, but they didn't seem like commanders or officers at all or as any people who were well-versed in warfare. No, they weren't. And we in the Serb Radical Party, especially Vojislav Seselj, we did not have any such aspirations, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take a very specific example, that of Vukovar. We know, because we've heard witnesses, we saw evidence, that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were in a unit in Vukovar. When SRS volunteers would be in a combat area, as in Vukovar, you were in Belgrade; did you know what was happening in realtime on the ground about combat operations or decisions that were made, or were you not aware of it? Did you only know that some individuals had been wounded or killed and that there had to be -- the bodies had to be brought back to Belgrade or that they had to be put into hospital in Belgrade? Could you tell us what you knew, based, for instance, on the example of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, well, I was one of the closest associates of Dr. Vojislav Seselj. I really don't know anything about these developments in the theatre of war. I only know about the things that you referred to during the second part of your question; that some people got killed, some people returned. That's the only thing I knew. So we in the Serb Radical Party, and I'm sure that that goes for Dr. Vojislav Seselj too, we did not have any insight into these operations; and this didn't really matter to us. What matters to us was that there was a force at the front-line, and that is the JNA and the Territorial Defence, defending our people, and we were there to help. Dr. Vojislav Seselj is consistent in respecting the setup of the state. With our volunteers or with any kind of activity of ours, he didn't want us to bring into question at all any of the legal and legitimate functions of the state itself, or any of the levers of state, especially such an important organisation like the JNA. That wouldn't have been rational, it wouldn't have been useful, but it wouldn't have been in accordance with our beliefs, or our programme, or our efforts to make sure that there is a proper state based on the rule of law, well set up, well established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, one last question before the break. We have heard many witnesses, we have seen a lot of evidence, that seems to boil down to this: Among the volunteers, there were some offenders who had been in prison, served sentences, and who overnight were released from jail in unknown circumstances and found themselves under the label of volunteers on battlefields, and of course they committed crimes. As far as you know, I'd like to know whether the SRS volunteers had been released from jail as part of a pardon or amnesty; and did you keep getting volunteers from a hard core of criminal offenders who were serving sentences and had been released in order to increase the number of men from the JNA or the TO? Are you aware of that, because it was told us, and we have heard testimony describing the behaviour of such individuals. Did you know that, did you not know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I participated in the organisation of the volunteers. What we checked was something that wasn't very difficult to check. It was some very -- very basic things; first of all, whether this volunteer had done his military service or had a criminal record, whether it was a person who had a regular sort of life. And from my area, really, there was no one like that. I mean, I'm sure that Mr. Seselj would not have allowed such people to go, because otherwise who would Dr. Vojislav Seselj be? Who would I be in the Serb Radical Party? We are following the oath of Kosovo, the traditions of the Chetnik Movement. And then I send criminals to loot out there or to slaughter Croats and Muslims, this is a pure fabrication. I'm deeply convinced of that. It is totally unacceptable. It does not belong to our core thinking. Please, we are looking at the destiny of our people, exposed to genocide. We are doing our best to help them. Now, would we do that with criminals? My brain cannot accept that, let alone my very political activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are challenging any statement of the kind, but you're adding one additional detail. You're saying that these volunteers were screened, if I could say so, because first they were checked to see whether they had done their military service, whether they had a regular sort of life, and whether they had ever been sanctioned. So in order to be volunteers, they had to be screened; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you know what, we were not a recruitment centre. It's not that we managed people in terms of height or whatever. We just looked at these basic elements in order to see who it was that was going out there to defend the people. What else, what else? We cannot send people to fight for the Serb people if, say, some of these persons are referred to as thieves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's time for our 20-minute break. I would like the Registrar to tell me how much time I've already spent, and we will meet again -- we'll resume in 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Court is resumed. Now, in direct line with my previous question, I would like to return to Vukovar, because I am looking at elements that are in the indictment. We know that Vukovar fell on November 18th. We know that 200 people were slaughtered in the -- at Ovcara on November 20, 1991. Mr. Seselj's case is the following: He says that the SRS volunteers left Vukovar before November 20th, and he told us, but so far he hasn't demonstrated this, he told us that he had testimonies from the bus drivers who drove the volunteers back before November 20th. So let's talk about the repatriation of volunteers after they left the battleground, repatriation by bus. I would like to know whether this was part of your mandate. Were you in charge of organising the repatriation of volunteers by bus? Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the problem is in the interpretation, but the interpretation I got was that there was no proof about the return of the volunteers before the 20th of November. And let me remind you that I showed you and the Prosecutor eight statements from drivers who drove the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I clearly said the following: Mr. Seselj told us that we had eight statements from bus drivers, stating that the volunteers had returned before November 20th. This is what Mr. Seselj said. Mr. Seselj said he had statements in this respect. Let me go back to my previous question. If volunteers are repatriated on buses, I would like to know whether you were involved in this operation, at least on the logistics side.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I personally was not involved, but I do remember a conversation with one of the volunteers from Pancevo. I remember his surname. It was Stojanovic, and he said that there was fierce fighting going on there, it was so fierce that they couldn't wait to go home, and that they went home immediately after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you were not involved in this, it must have been the War Staff who looked into this repatriation of these volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, regarding volunteers, I would like to know the following: When a volunteer, sent on the battlefield, committed an offence, whatever the offence, was the Serbian Radical Party informed of this? And if so, what was the sanction involved?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, Dr. Vojislav Seselj was very strict when it came to infractions and violations of discipline, and I remember that whenever he sent volunteers off and whenever there was any discussion about the activities of the volunteers, in addition to the principles of chivalrous behaviour and noble behaviour, he would always stress the respect that the Serb volunteers had to demonstrate, and he always insisted upon discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not put any questions to you regarding Mr. Seselj's speech on May 6th, 1992, at Hrtkovci, because you said in your statement that this was the St. Sava and that day you stayed home. However, I would like to talk about the exchange of flats. We heard a good number of witnesses here who told us that the Serbs had been expelled from Croatia. Allegedly, there would have been 200.000 of them. Some went to Vojvodina, and the Croats and Serbs seem to have exchanged flats. Now, as far as the leadership of the SRS is concerned, were you aware of this exchange of flats?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: We did know about it, and Dr. Vojislav Seselj insisted on having this exchange of flats and property and that nobody should be at a disadvantage and disadvantaged, as far as that was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were aware of it. Very well. Was this a deliberate desire on --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... undertaken by the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were aware of it. But did the SRS and Mr. Seselj deliberately decide to ensure that this exchange of flats would actually take -- exist?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Correct. Dr. Seselj insisted on that. Seselj always looks a long way ahead, and his goal is that the Croats, those who at one time converted to Catholicism and became Croats one day, should understand this and accept this and be part of a joint nation again. Dr. Seselj was not in favour of any kind of violence or any kind of revenge, especially not persecution or genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now going to move into more sensitive issues. Of course, all issues are sensitive, but some more so than others, and I'm about to delve into very crucial matters. You made a written statement after you were interviewed for four days in 2003. Obviously, at the time -- well, not obviously. I would like to know whether you knew at the time that this statement would be used in the proceedings against Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I took it seriously, the statement with the Hague investigators, but from the beginning of my talks with the investigators, right up to my conversation with Ms. Christine Dahl, I always stressed that I did not wish to be a Prosecution witness, or a witness at all, for that matter, because I did not take part in the war, I was not on the battle front, I know of no crimes, and I know of no -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when you signed this statement, you said that you wanted to contribute to the manifestation of truth, but you did not deliberately say that you wanted to be a Defence witness. I have the statement here in my hands, and there is no mention of this.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: My position was this: Not to go and testify, not to take part in this trial. But I decided to be a Defence witness after having talked to Ms. Christine Dahl. I talked to her and the investigator, Paolo Stocchi. I held that discussion last year on the 16th of November. And I'll tell you why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You left the SRS in 1994. Could you tell me why you left this party, and what was the difference of opinion that forced you to leave the party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Two reasons. The first is this: The people who surrounded Dr. Seselj, his closest associates, were people without any ideals and visions, ideas, without the capability -- without capabilities, people who had no successful work behind them, either on the political scene or in science or anything else, but were overtly ambitious and narcissistic. And they didn't like me, either. They had some animosity towards me. I'm a different man altogether, of different experience and different structure. So that was the main reason. That they were people without any visions and ideas, well, I can provide ample evidence to show that. When they left Dr. Seselj, for example, they didn't do anything -- give anything back to the public. They engage in politics with some other political programmes. It includes some other people, people who just talk about the European Union, in fact just following the programme of some other political party. Boris Tadic's, in fact, to be specific. So those are the kind of people I didn't want to associate with. The second reason is Dr. Seselj, when the Serbian Radical Party was under a total media blockade by the Socialist Party and Slobodan Milosevic's regime, Dr. Seselj, in order to be heard publicly, behaved as he did in the Assembly and caused incidents. He asked me to pour water over Radovan Bozovic. I couldn't accept that. He wanted to cause these media effects, and I couldn't do this to Bozovic. I know him, I know that he gained riches, but not on the basis of what's work; and now the papers are writing and saying that he's the head of the Montenegrin mafia, which is the strongest mafia in Serbia, which is destroying the Serb economy and Serb spiritual being, too. So those are the two reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You gave us your two reasons, and we can now move on to the next topic which I wanted to address. When you were interviewed by the investigators of the OTP, these investigators were asking questions about the financing and the funding of the SRS. Could you tell us how the Serbian Radical Party operated, as far as funding is concerned and revenues?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: What I know is this: When the Serbian Chetnik Movement was founded, we were financed from the funds Seselj managed to -- through his activities in Western countries, in Australia, America, and in Canada, from those proceedings, as president of the Chetnik Movement and as a Serbian intellectual. Later on, when the elections were held in 1992, I had my own sponsors for my own area, and from Branko Djukic, near Banja Luka, who was in the oil business, we were given a whole truckload of petrol, a 30-tonne truck. So there were people like that who helped us out with fuel and other things. Otherwise, it wasn't my field of expertise. I didn't have any insight into the treasury, or funds, or anything like that. But in one of my books, it says that I said that the Serb Radical Movement of Dr. Vojislav Seselj was given 10 million in cooperation with Milosevic and so on and so forth. Well, that's just an expression of my impotence, my powerlessness and my response to certain assertions. Once I left the Serbian Radical Party and when the Serbian Radical Party and Dr. Seselj too, he maligned me and they maligned me; and they said I was an idiot and a traitor, and that I had sold my soul, and things like that. In addition to all that, they said that I had been given 5 million German marks on Cyprus. And then I responded with equal measure, and I said that they had been given 10 million. And that's the kind of thing we do in Serbia in these political conflicts. We ascribe to the opposite side certain things that are really not true. It's not true that I got 5 million marks. Had I had that money, I would be a big businessman, but I live in Serbia and retired. I live off my pension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On paragraph 83 of your statement, you told the interviewers that Stefanovic had told you that Milosevic had funded either Seselj or the Serbian Radical Party, had actually given this party or Mr. Seselj 1 million Deutsche mark for the support of an election. Does this mean that Slobodan Milosevic was actually funding the Serbian Radical Party? It seems that that's what you hint at in paragraph 83, and you say that you heard this from Stefanovic and this was actually in one of your books.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I cannot substantiate that with anything, and it's even difficult to believe. It's difficult to believe in that, since Slobodan Milosevic blocked the party, incarcerated Dr. Seselj. Now, this piece of information in my book, what I wrote there, well, it's just rumour, I was just rumour-mongering because of my powerlessness, so I wanted to inflict some damage, malign them as retaliation for what they had said about me in the Serbian Radical Party once I had left the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that the information revealed in your book should be, in fact -- it's just a settlement -- it's just ascribed to a settlement and it's rumours, actually, more than anything; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth of it, that's the real truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I would like to have -- I would like to know something. Are you saying that what you wrote in your books is not to be trusted?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: It's not credible, that -- and I can't prove it, and I'm not proud of having written that, of having stooped in a period of my life to the level of the desire to get my own back. I shouldn't have done that. Certainly, it's a bad episode in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to shed some light on something you told the OTP, and let me sum it up. The International Community had placed an embargo on oil imports, and you said that the Serbian Radical Party had a company that made it possible to bypass this embargo and to sell oil in former Yugoslavia, and which helped the Serbian Radical Party obtain revenue at the time by selling this oil. You said that, but are you challenging this today or do you maintain this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, that company was in existence for a very brief period of time. Dr. Seselj conditionally accepted the work of this company, but when he saw that business dealings like that were not commensurate with the party image, he gave up on it, and it was closed down. Now, later on, through my sponsor, I managed to secure enough fuel for the elections in 1992, but that sponsor imported fuel himself, petrol himself. He made a lot of money, and he's a very wealthy businessman. You can find him near Banja Luka, at a petrol pump there. So had it not been this black marketeering through Bulgaria, especially Serbia would have had no fuel, and it would have put a stop to the economy and life in general; so you had to find a way to get around the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also involved one of Mr. Seselj's relatives, his former bodyguard, Petar Panic. According to you, he was controlling the black market, notably when it came to currency exchange. Is it true or false?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Mr. Paolo Stocchi talked about that during the interview. I couldn't confirm it then, either. Now, what he put on record, I don't know. The records were kept for four days. The interview took place for four days. We had an interpreter. Mr. Paolo Stocchi has a special way of asking questions. He asks you a question and then provides the answer; and then he says who he got the information from and so forth. Now, I gave my answer, and what he put into the statement, into the record, I don't know. That Petar Panic had worked with foreign current, I can't confirm that, nor do I have any insight in the work of Petar Panic at all. He was a bodyguard to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one final question on this issue, and it has to do with Mrs. Seselj. Paragraph 92 of your statement, you explain that Mr. Seselj would have received about US $50 million to enter into the government in coalition with the SPS, and then you add that Mrs. Seselj, Jadranka Seselj, owned an import/export company and that since her husband was vice-president of the government of Serbia, that made it possible for her to obtain a competitive advantage for her company. So do you still maintain this or do you challenge it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I had absolutely no means of knowing about any dealings -- business dealings that Mrs. Seselj might have had at the time, or about Mr. Seselj receiving any money from the Socialist Party. At that time, I was not involved in politics. I was engaged in some other affairs. I was leading quite a different life. Now, Paolo Stocchi talked about that, and I assume he recorded it, too, because he wanted to, because let me repeat, that's his style of interviewing. He asked the questions, provides the answers. Now, what goes down in the record, I really can't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you signed what is written in paragraph 92. We have your initials on the minutes -- on the statement.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I signed on the fourth day, without reading through the minutes, the statement. And when Mr. Paolo Stocchi told me that he'd be interviewing me some more if I refused to sign, I did refuse to sign. However, he sort of prevailed upon me and forced me to sign in that way. And his way of conducting an interview, well, does not accord with the rules of procedure or is not according to legal provisions. He has a cowboy way of interrogating, interviewing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently after you left the SRS, you were accused of being a traitor, and that is what is stated. And then we get the impression that at one point in time, people around Mr. Seselj tried to kidnap either your wife or your daughter, which is just something you said. Now, could you tell us exactly what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what happened. The truth of the matter is this: Near my flat at the time, several men stopped my wife. They wanted to get her into their car.
