However, afterwards we learnt and established -- that is to say, my associate called people up from the Serbian Radical Party to see what was going on, and they said it had nothing to do with the Serbian Radical Party or with Dr. Seselj. And I know full well that Dr. Seselj uses [as interpreted] methods like that, nor does he need to. What would he achieve, after all? He would achieve a negative effect. It would have a negative effect, as far as he was concerned and as far as his party was concerned. So this was done by people arbitrarily who said that they had links to the Serbian Radical Party. But we checked this out and found that they had nothing to do with the leadership of the Serbian Radical Party at all, and especially not with Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, at paragraph 129 of your statement made with the investigators of the OTP -- you know, nothing escapes me, and I scrutinised this document for hours, I poured over it for hours. Well, at paragraph 129, you said the following: At the beginning of 1995, members of the SRS, led by Zoran Drazilovic, came in front of your apartment in Belgrade, in a number of cars, and surrounded your wife on the street and tried to drag her into the car. One of your neighbours intervened and defended your wife. And then you explain this action was done against you because Seselj wanted to punish you for having left the party. So here you actually named Zoran Drazilovic and incriminated him, so what can you say today regarding this affair?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I didn't see Zoran Drazilovic. My wife assumed that it was him, but we later learnt that it wasn't Zoran Drazilovic or anybody else from the leadership of the Serbian Radical Party, nor did anybody from the Serbian Radical Party issue orders to that effect. And I know that Mr. Seselj condemned that kind of behaviour, and they weren't people that were responsible for politics and the actions of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now move to the fact that at one point in time, you decided to be a Defence witness. How did this happen? Did you suddenly say, "Why be a Prosecution witness when I could be a Defence witness?" Could you tell us exactly what train of thought you had at the time in order to end up with this decision?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, the following reasons, Mr. President: On the 16th of September, 2006, Mr. Dan Saxon came to see me. We had an hour-long conversation, or a little longer, in fact, in a very pleasant atmosphere; and I managed to convince Mr. Saxon that I could not be a witness that would be of any use to the Prosecution, because I didn't take part in the war, nor do I know about any war crimes, and at the same time I said I believe that Dr. Seselj -- well, Mr. Saxon said: "Very well. If you cannot testify about war crimes, come and help us to politically liquidate Dr. Vojislav Seselj, because Dr. Vojislav Seselj is the greatest danger to the new authorities in Serbia." And he stressed that we must ensure the kind of authorities -- authority and power that would be pro-Western, a pro-Western government. And I said that I wasn't going to take part in that, either, of course. But what was particularly important, as far as I was concerned, was something that Mr. Saxon said. He said: "Well, if you refuse and if all the others who we thought would testify against Dr. Seselj refuse, then the question arises, and I don't personally believe that Dr. Seselj will be convicted and punished." That's what he said. That's the -- and I personally have no evidence against him. So, well, I got through that, I lived through that. They're prosecutors, they prosecute, they have their goals and tasks. They seem to be more political than legal, to my mind. But finally I decided, after working with Ms. Dahl, to come in. And when I told Ms. Dahl the same thing I told Mr. Saxon, I said that I cannot be -- could not be a Prosecution witness, Dr. Seselj did not commit any crimes, she was resigned and said, "Well, you're refusing, everybody's refusing, so what am I going to do with the indictment? Seselj will go back, then." And she also said, "You can speak neutrally what you wrote in your statement." And I don't know what is in the statement. And then she said, "When you come to The Hague, we'll decide about Ovcara and Vocin." And then afterwards I saw that they want to convict an innocent man, that they want to convict somebody for ideology and politics which are the ideology and politics that I share. Well, you're not going to do that, you Western people. We're not impotent, we Serbs. So when you're pilfering us and looting us, you say, "Isn't that nice." When you kill us, we're supposed to say, "Go ahead, kill us some more." Well, you can't do it that way. I am going to defend my Serb, Vojislav Seselj. And nobody from the Serbian Radical Party initiated any agreement or interview. I initiated a talk with Zoran Krasic after words with Petar Jojic, and I have nothing to hide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you took the initiative. I am --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, believe me, I left Seselj, and you know what my activity after that was. It is so obvious that no one can influence my activity and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to know this. Do you have a political activity today or have you stopped altogether?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Now, I'm a member of the Serb Radical Party, and I'm a member of the Municipal Assembly of the Town of Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you were elected a member of Parliament at the last elections, and you are an SRS member, and you are, as such, a member of Parliament?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: No, I was on the ticket of the Serb Radical Party as of May. After speaking to Ms. Dahl and after this visit paid by this lady on the 28th of February this year, this lady introduced herself as a Slovene, I can describe her, whatever her name was, she came into my apartment, she entered almost by force; and she said that she was a friend of this Court. And she opened her bag full of foreign currency, and I threw her out. Well, you know what? I cannot work in favour of a prosecutor that is prepared to do all of these things that I've told you about until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were elected into Parliament?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: No, no. After this visit, and I gave this a great deal of thought, and since I had prepared a new book in which I viewed the position of the Serb people in global terms, and generally speaking I look at global relations, this is a rather serious book with rather serious aspirations, I realised and I am convinced that the only authentic Serb politician now is Dr. Vojislav Seselj. In Serbia, we have another politician who is prepared to defend the interests of his state and his people, and that is Vojislav Kostunica. However, Dr. Seselj is closer to me, in terms of his programme and ideology, and I'm prepared to fight for this ideology and this policy until the end of my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say that you want to fight for this ideology. Well, this brings me to a possible link between Milosevic, Seselj, and Karadzic. As far as you know, did Mr. Seselj meet with Mr. Milosevic ?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about any specific meeting, but Dr. Seselj didn't call me or inform me about that meeting. However, what I'm sure of is that Milosevic was a bit afraid of Dr. Seselj as a competitor in the field of government. Dr. Seselj always fully expressed the truth about policies, about mistakes made, about good things done by Milosevic, and he did not, therefore, depend on Milosevic at all, or on anyone else, for that matter. As for Milosevic, I don't think he's a traitor, but that he does not have the right format to be able to lead Serbia and the Serbian people. He, himself, admitted at the 2nd or 3rd Congress of the Socialist Party that he had not made the right estimate of the international factor. That is impermissible. It is an impermissible short coming, as far as a politician is concerned, and also the detriment is incalculable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, what about links with Radovan Karadzic? What were they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of any intensive relations between Dr. Seselj and Dr. Karadzic. What I do know is that Dr. Karadzic is a politician of a similar mettle like Milosevic. He did not like competition, and he steered clear of Dr. Vojislav Seselj; and he did not want him to have an influence over the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, as far as the defence of the Serbian people is concerned, sending soldiers to Republika Srpska, there was some cooperation, of course. Karadzic or Ratko Mladic would not allow Seselj to interfere in their conduct of war, or would Dr. Seselj meddle in that kind of thing. Like in the case of Croatia, he just wanted to help in the defence of the Serb people, and he did not set up any radical formations of his own. After all, in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was an independent Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last topic I'd like to address with you, Greater Serbia. You mentioned this in paragraph 104 of your statement. In your view, what was the outlook -- the concept Mr. Seselj had of the Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: A Greater Serbia is a concept, a concept of the historical and national rights of the Serb people. As for this concept and this ideology, Dr. Seselj elaborated it in a complete fashion, and he proved how, during the 19th and 20th century, Serbs disassociated themselves from their own nation, and that process is going on to this day. According to the information from last year, already 50.000 Serbs in Croatia do not dare declare themselves as Serbs or as Orthodox Christians. They don't want to abandon their ethnic and religious background, but as the state organs and the Catholic Church in Croatia that are making them do that. They were Serbs, they registered them as Croats. They were Orthodox Christians, they registered them as Catholics. In my studies, I obtained some data, and I could not get a hold of all the data that Dr. Seselj had, that, for example, according to our well-known historian, Dragoljub Zivojinovic, before the Second World War there were 1.900.000 Serbs in Croatia. How many are there now, about 200.000 in Croatia. Please, if a person is to be serious, if a scholar is to be serious, a doctor, a professor, a doctor of sciences like Dr. Seselj, can he not take that into account when elaborating his concept? These are the historic and national rights of the Serb people. Dr. Seselj insists on that; namely, that that will be achieved through an evolution. One day, this information is going to be made available to all Croats, those who used to be Serbs and those who were not Serbs. Dr. Seselj is counting on that. He's also counting on stronger Slavism, that Slavism affirm its strength so that it's a partner to Western Europe, not to have Slavism curtailed through Poles and Croats. I think that Dr. Seselj is proceeding from real, proven facts, and that he basis his concepts and ideology on them. He does not advocate, on the basis of his information, his knowledge, his research, his books, he does not advocate conflict with other peoples. He does not advocate genocide or conflict. He is responsible, in terms of the truth and science.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to the concept of pan-Slavism, I read with interest that you are the author of some papers on the Constitution. As a lawyer, I'm sure you will understand the gist of my question. Is one of the consequences of pan-Slavism that territories, frontiers, can be shifted, or is it just a cultural concept, a humanist concept or a religious one that does not bring with itself any changes in territory, that does not result in borders being changed, territory being given, and is this concept compatible with Yugoslavia's -- former Yugoslavia's administrative structures? What is your thought, your estimate of the situation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Antonetti, precisely, we do not advocate any kind of secession, any kind of violent change of borders. I personally would like it if we had the right kind of situation of renewing Yugoslavia, but certainly not to -- not at the expense of the Serb people or any other people. Of course, for the time being, that is impossible. What I personally advocate, as an academician and as a citizen, is that Slav countries cooperate to the best of their ability on the basis of mutual interests of Slavic countries. In my academy, we do study this subject matter. We study the specific characteristics of the Slav peoples and also what we have in common, in terms of tradition, language, culture, the economy and politics. We do offer such solutions; inter alia, we prepared an agreement on the establishment of a Slavic community. Of course, that cannot move ahead fast, but that is our vision. All these capacities should be used, and why not use the experience of Western Europe too, when Western Europe organised itself very nicely and everyone benefits from that? Why would Slav peoples not do that, too, not on the basis of superiority and inferiority, as is now being imposed through the European Union and NATO? Why would Serbia be in NATO now, and then they bombed us in 1999. They say we're friends. Yeah, right, friends, friends who bomb us. Why would we not create that kind of community, and why would not be -- why would we not be partners very nicely in peace with the West and avail ourselves of all this experience? Why would we not trade? Why would we not base relations on that concept? Why not? And then this concept of the great de Gaulle, who we Serbs highly respect, Europe from the Atlantic to the Ural Mountains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. I can tell you that, but I guess you know. You know that in the indictment against Mr. Seselj, a joint criminal enterprise is alleged, the purpose of which is to create a Greater Serbia whose western borders would tally with the Karlobag-Karlovac-Ogulin-Virovitica axis; and that therefore this Greater Serbia had to take territory from Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina for it to be fulfilled. This is what the Prosecutor said in the indictment. What do you think of this theory of a Greater Serbia with the Karlobag-to-Virovitica line?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this line or axis was not invented by Dr. Seselj. It was the French and the English who established it in 1915, when Serbia put up a strong resistance against Austria and Germany in the First World War, and when they were the allies of the Serb people and the Serb state, and when they had a realistic view of the interests of the Serb people. They took into account all of these facts and elements that Dr. Seselj explained in his books. That is the historic right of the Serb people. Of course, I accept that this is a historic and national right of the Serb people, but I also accept the way in which this could perhaps be carried through on the basis of evolution and a long-term process, like Dr. Seselj. Dr. Seselj did not call for a creation of a Greater Serbia through showdowns, war, persecutions, crimes, or genocide. He pointed this out as rights. He cautioned the Croatian people, "If you persecute us Serbs, if you kill us, if you kill us for no reason whatsoever, in a groundless fashion, these are our rights." However, during the course of the war, Dr. Seselj never spoke about volunteers, or did he ask the JNA to go out and establish this kind of a Greater Serbia. He just indicated this, and he cautioned the Croats and the rest in Yugoslavia. Well, we have this historic right, and after all, we advocated Yugoslavia, and we would not have raised this issue had Yugoslavia still been in existence. We only raised this issue in terms of defending the Serb people from genocide, which they did experience, nevertheless, in the territory of Croatia. I don't think that on the basis of this concept or this ideology, Seselj advocated war, persecutions and genocide. That is my view, and I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now turning to the Prosecution. You have one hour. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have one moment just to reorganise.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think it's still morning. Good morning, Mr. Glamocanin.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My name is Lisa Biersay. We have not met, have we?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: We haven't, no, but I've seen you. I've seen you in TV coverage from these trials, and you seem to be very fair and very professional. Now, whether you're going to be that way remains to be seen now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll try my best. You described to the Court your first involvement with the SRS. Do you remember that description you gave for the Court?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I told you I was in the Serb Chetnik Movement, and the Serb Radical Party came into being when the Serb Chetnik Movement united with the People's Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Sir, do you need glasses in order to read?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I wanted to show you a document on the screen. And let me know if it would be easier to see the hard copy, but I think it will work. If I could have 65 ter number 84, please. I'd like to direct your attention to February of 1991. Was that the time of the founding of the SRS, as you described it? Is that date correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is the time of the founding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you were -- it was at that founding where you were elected a member of the board of the SRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Also, there were members of the -- you describe the Serbian Chetnik Movement; namely Petkovic and Gojkovic and Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, Petkovic, yes. Gojkovic, Nikolic, I think they were from the People's Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there also representatives from the NRS?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: NRS meaning "Narodna Radikalna Stranka," People's Radical Party. Well, that's it, Nikolic and Gojkovic, and I can't remember who else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you look at your screen, and are you able to make it out from where you're sitting? The B/C/S version should be on your left.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could go to the title page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, this is the Statute of the Serbian Chetnik Movement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for the Court, this was published in, I believe, July -- on July 1st, 1990, in 'Velika Srbija.' At this time, the Prosecution would move for the -- move for the admission of 65 ter number 84, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you sure that this has not yet been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: According to my assessment, Your Honour, it has not been. I think there was another document with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I can remember, this has been admitted. It was admitted during the testimony of Expert Theunens, if my memory serves me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I thought, too. I thought it had been admitted. Let's have a number. If there were two numbers, if there were to be two numbers, we'll just erase one. A number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P868. Thank you, Your Honour. Excuse me, correction for the transcript. This shall be given Exhibit number P686. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could please go to paragraph 12 of that exhibit, please, or Article 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's on the next page. It's coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The print is very small.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it possible to enlarge on just the B/C/S side that section 12?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it. It has been enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in Article 12, am I correct in saying that is an outline of the organisation of the party, of the movement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what can be seen. In all of these areas, there are Serbs, but not only Serbs. There are inhabitants of all other ethnicities living in those areas that were members of this organisation of ours, so it's not an exclusively Serb organisation. Let me remind you of something else. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One minute, one minute. We'll get to that. I just wanted to ask you if, in that article, it names several regional administrations, correct, for the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you described for the Court your tenure as president of the Regional Board of Banat, the Court asked you where that was, how many districts did the Banat region cover?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, Serbia is not organised on the basis of districts, but counties, rather; municipalities, counties and provinces. There are three counties with centres in Pancevo, Zrenjanin and Kikinda, respectively. At the time when I was president of the Regional Board, there were these three counties. To this day, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for those three districts, there was a president for each one; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. A double objection, at that. First of all, Ms. Biersay intentionally confuses the Serb Chetnik Movement and the Serb Radical Party. Secondly, this is the Statute of the Serb Chetnik Movement from 1990, not only during the existence of Yugoslavia, but also during the existence of communist regime, and at that time there was no law on the territorial organisation of Serbia on the basis of counties. That law was passed, I think, in 1991, if I remember correctly, or perhaps even in 1992. So this is arbitrary, these regions set out here, and they're not supported by any kind of administrative acts on the part of the state. This is intentional confusion that is being created, and I simply had to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, obviously the document here does not address the Serbian Radical Party, but the Serb Chetnik Movement. And, secondly, according to Mr. Seselj, this document dates back to 1990, and as far as the administrative breakdown of Serbia was concerned, there were no districts at the time, or that's what he's saying, anyway. And the witness seems to be nodding and confirming what Mr. Seselj is saying. Please proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I omitted to take that fact into account. I was speaking from the aspects of the internal division of Serbia at the time when I became involved in the -- actively in the work of the Serbian Radical Party, and present day conditions. Yes, Mr. Seselj is actually right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would respectfully request that to the extent that Mr. Seselj has clarifying questions, that he waits until his opportunity to examination the witness, instead of interrupting me and making his arguments for which the witness is supposed to adapt his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, I fully agree with you, but then if you are going astray, you know, on an erroneous assumption, then everybody is wasting time. So it's best, you know, to put you back on track immediately, rather than let you waste 15 to 20 minutes on a subject, and then afterwards, in about 20 seconds, he can destroy all the arguments you put forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, it's not my arguments, it's testimony coming from the witness, and Mr. Glamocanin has shown he's more than capable of correcting me if I need to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In addition to these -- the districts that you described, and you also mentioned that there are municipalities as well within the region over which you had the Presidency -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I can't tell you much about this. Yes, I was a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. However, at that time, right up until September 1991, I was active in another movement, and I was the head of that movement, and that was the Solidarity Alliance of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand, I understand. You, in addition to setting up and taking oversight of this region, you also described how you assembled experts, is that correct, to set up economic programmes, like education and infrastructure and health for your region? You initiated all of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Along with cooperation -- agreement from Mr. Seselj, we rallied -- I rallied experts, and we made an economic programme for the Serbian Radical Party based on ideas or, rather, ideology, and that programme was added on to later on and modified.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described for the Court the SRS branches that existed in the other republics. Was there also an SRS branch of Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, Vojvodina is part of Serbia, and I was at the head of the movement which did a great deal and helped a great deal to have Vojvodina back within the composition of Serbia. We didn't make any separate organisation for Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could now have 65 ter number 7427, and I'd like the last page, please. Actually, I believe it's 7427A, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that document, sir, the War Staff, if we could talk about the War Staff. You described the War Staff as part of the central structure of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, for me, that staff was a service dealing with affairs related to the departure of volunteers, their accommodation, taking them in; but it wasn't only the War Staff of the Serbian Radical Party that did things like that, but taking in these people as linked to the JNA activities. The JNA, as has been proved here, brought all the volunteers in buses. They were brought back to Belgrade. Some came to the War Staff, others didn't. Then that War Staff also helped in the following way: They helped them record their war service, that is to say, the time they had spent on the battle front, and so on and so forth, the benefits and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe that you did describe that for the Trial Chamber. My question to you is: Was the War Staff one of the bodies of the Serbian Chetnik Movement or was it separate from the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: No, the Serbian Chetnik Movement did not exist at that time, at the time when the volunteers went to the battle front. It was the Serbian Radical Party that existed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did the Serbian Chetnik Movement come into existence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seselj has already said that, and you said in 1990, mid-1990, but there were the so-called Young Chetniks in Serbia before the Serbian Chetnik Movement. I know that full well because my own son was the president of those Young Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On the document before you, which is 65 ter number 7427A, can you see -- can you see what's on the right side -- the left side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: It says "Main Board" there, and then there's some signatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, Madam, I didn't take part in these affairs, so I can't really tell you anything about that. All I can do is read out what it says. But other than that, to say that I remember the document, no. And to say what it's all about, I really can't do that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: May I ask that a hard copy of this document be given to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If you could flip to the very back, the last page.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, my handwriting, but I don't remember this. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But you recognise your handwriting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I just can't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you described to the Trial Chamber that the vice-president for Republika Srpska was a Poplasen, and perhaps I'm not pronouncing that correctly.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see here, Nikola Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you also described the vice-president at that time for the SRS in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, Radovan Vucevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At the local level, when we're talking about the coordination of volunteers at the local level, was that coordination done by Serbian Chetnik Movement members?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: At this level, at the level that I was in the party, we had a man in charge of working with the volunteers, and I assisted him. He organised work with them. I helped him out. I thought it was my duty to do so, and also I had the desire to help. And he coordinated work with people who were in charge of the same affairs at party level.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was his official title, if he had one? The person that you're -- do you know someone by the name of Stefan Grubanov [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Stefan Grubanov, yes. Well, he worked through the volunteers, matters related to the volunteers. He had his own office, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did he coordinate the volunteers for your area?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He dealt with all those matters, and he coordinated, but I assisted as president of the Regional Board and later on as president of the County Board, and I was in a position to help him. Of course, I didn't make the lists, I didn't do these administrative things, but the serious matters. When I say "serious," I mean when the volunteers had to go to a church and take Holy Communion and pledge that they would fight chivalrously in the eyes of God, that they would not commit evil deeds. And of course when it was necessary to secure some funds from the business community, from the state and so on, I was better placed to do things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, this coordinator of the volunteers, did he report to you or did he report to the War Staff in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, the War Staff, establishment-wise. But he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party, so that we cooperated intensively, but I wasn't interested nor did I have the duty to deal with all the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that within each local SRS branch, there was a local coordinator who would deal with the volunteers in the capacity like Mr. Grubanov did?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, not every municipality had that, but in the Banat area I'm quite sure it did; Pancevo, Zrenjanin, and Kikinda, and that's an area which was the most successful in terms of numbers and in all the other aspects linked to the volunteers' departure to the battle front. And let me also tell you that in Pancevo and everywhere else, we had quite a lot of Hungarian volunteers, there would be a few Romanians, so that the defence both of the Serb people and the desire to defend and protect Yugoslavia, too, was something that was accepted by one and all, all the ethnic groups. We had Hungarians, for example, who laid down their lives, who were killed in Pancevo. We had people who were wounded and injured, and there was a general atmosphere of -- well, a very enviable atmosphere with respect to the work of the Serbian Radical Party and its standing up in defence of the Serb people in those war-infested areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: With respect to the Serbian Chetnik Movement, who was at the head of that movement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: While it was functioning, it was Dr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did those people who were given the title vojvodas have within the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Some of the vojvodas were linked to the battle front. Others acted politically as members of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you ever a vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: No, I never became a vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I didn't have any pretensions along those lines, either. Well, that's why. I don't have any pretensions as somebody fighting on the front. I am engaged in other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So the vojvodas were the force behind the armed struggle of the SRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's not correct that the SRS was a combat force. It all functioned in the way in which we've already discussed today. We would send volunteers, but it wasn't the SRS or the Serbian Chetnik Movement that had its own units. They were units within the composition of the legal forces; first of all, the JNA, then later on the Territorial Defence, and later on still the army of Republika Srpska Krajina was formed, and then in Bosnia-Herzegovina the army of the -- of Republika Srpska was formed. And before that -- well, yes, the army of Republika Srpska was formed there straight away, and they had their own Territorial Defence for a short period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I didn't want to interrupt the witness, but I have an objection to make once the witness finishes what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj has lost the opportunity to object to the question if it's already been answered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have the right to object to a question within the frameworks of the general conduct of the Prosecutor. It's not my intention to control how the Prosecutor's going to use her time. It's in my interest if the Prosecutor wastes her time. But it has to be conducted properly, because the Prosecutor has the right to trick questions as well, but he does not have the right to ask questions which will create confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I submit to the Chamber that Mr. Seselj is now giving cues to the witness on how to answer, and it's inappropriate for him to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I waited for the witness to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'm trying to understand your objection. Ms. Biersay is putting questions to this witness on vojvodas. He answers that he never was a vojvoda, and now you're taking the floor for something that I don't understand what your point is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I intentionally waited for the witness to complete his answer so as not to influence his answer. I'm intervening because I consider that any examination must, in principle, be conducted properly and correctly. Ms. Biersay asked whether the Chetnik vojvodas were the basic force in the war, and she knows full well that the first Chetnik vojvodas on my part were proclaimed in May 1993, and the war had been going on for two years already. So that is that improper conduct that permeates her manner of examination, and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Biersay, Mr. Seselj is saying that the vojvodas he appointed were proclaimed in May 1993, and that, therefore, you cannot ask the witness whether the vojvodas played a role previously. He says that they were only proclaimed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, according to our procedure in this Tribunal, you can ask questions on this, but during your own cross-examination, and you can ask the witness to give details and specific answers on this and maybe correct what he answered to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something else? It is not my intention to ask the witness to clarify these matters, because this witness can't know everything, but a document has already been admitted into evidence. It was signed by my hand, about the proclamation of the first Chetnik vojvodas in May 1993, whereas -- so the Prosecutor cannot behave as if there's been none of that, none of those proceedings so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I regret, Mr. Seselj, if the witness does not know, during the cross-examination he will just answer one of your questions by saying, "I don't know." But you're not allowed to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now if we could please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I would like to have my position on the transcript regarding this issue. The Court's time, the Bench's time, is very precious. You know that. I had two hours, and in these two hours I put all my questions. The Prosecutor will have one hour and Mr. Seselj will have one hour. So everyone intervening, be it a Judge, the accused or the Prosecutor, must be absolutely sure of his question when he puts it. He must be absolutely sure of the basis of his question, because if he makes a mistake, then there are consequences; raises objections and so forth and so on. So as far as this question of vojvodas, which we have already explored at length with many other witnesses, I believe, Ms. Biersay, that if you have elements that may allow you to say that in 1991, there were -- or 1992, there were vojvodas actually acting on the ground, then do so, but you have to be very specific. You have to be able to back what you say. Otherwise, we're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd now like to direct your attention to 65 ter number 92, and hopefully you'll be able to read that. And while we're retrieving that, it's an article entitled "The Leader of Zvezda's Delijas Has Joined the Serbian Chetnik Movement," and this was published in 'Velika Srbija,' issued number 2, 1990. And if we could go to the bottom of the B/C/S. Could we go to the next page, please, for the B/C/S. And in the lower corner, lower right-hand corner, if you could enlarge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Actually, do you recognise -- I know it's a grainy picture, but you discussed your son being in one of the -- in one of the groups?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, my son.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I do. Srdjan, I recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could please enlarge that box. And I believe the corresponding English would be on page -- there we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, the title of that is "The Vojvoda Dr. Vojislav Seselj's Oath"; is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I have never seen this oath, but I have no reason to doubt -- doubt it, and it is an oath within the frameworks of the traditions of the Serbian people and the traditions of all those who loved their people and who were ready to die for their people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: 'Velika Srbija' is a publication associated with what party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, that's already been stated. This 'Velika Srbija' is still published, and it's becoming a better and better newspaper. It has a lot of scholarly articles and very -- has been successful, and it's far and above the best paper throwing light on all topical issues and the overall problems that face the Serb nation and the Serb state, and also the world situation, world affairs, and all the rest of it, and men of letters and men of science write for the papers, academicians, university professors, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time, the Prosecution moves for admission of 65 ter number 92, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I think -- I think my objection is in order. In the previous issue of 'Velika Srbija,' the Prosecutor had at its disposal a whole article about my taking the oath of the Serbian Chetnik vojvoda in Libertyville Monastery near Chicago in the United States of America. There was an extensive article about all that. And in the next issue, they just repeat the oath. So why doesn't the Prosecutor tender into evidence both, because like this you don't know where the oath was taken, on what occasion, or anything else. It's just something that's been inserted there. And they have all the documents, they have all the back issues of 'Velika Srbija,' so why don't they tender both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know it now. You just told us where it was done. Let's have a number for this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P687. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, inquire as to how much time I have left and when the Court would like to take its next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the Registrar, because I don't know. You have 30 minutes. I think it's best to break right now, and we'll resume later on. Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Twenty-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Before I ask Ms. Biersay to proceed, Witness, I seek a small clarification. You said that you were elected a member of Parliament. I'd like to know this: Were you elected at the level of the Pancevo municipality or were you elected a member of the Parliament in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I was an MP from 1992 until the end of 1996, but I've been a member of the Municipal Assembly since May this year. And I returned to the Serb Radical Party, rejoined its ranks, in March this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are a regional member of Parliament in the Pancevo municipality to date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am still a member of the Municipal Assembly from the elections that were held in May this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be a problem with the interpretation. What I want to know is this: I want to know whether you are a member of Parliament in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all I want to know. The rest, you are a local member or elected person, you were elected locally. That's all I wanted to know. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could now have Exhibit P223, please. And just for planning purposes, after that I'll also ask for P227, P217, and P25.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, you'll need your glasses, because I'll be showing you some documents on that computer screen again.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So that would be Exhibit P223. Now, isn't it true that the volunteers were deployed as units and not just incorporated into existing JNA units as individuals? And looking at P223, it reads: "On behalf of SRS volunteer units, Commander Novacic is authorised to coordinate on behalf of the SRS, Podravska Slatina TOS Staff relating to the defence, manpower and other needs. The commander shall be recalled at the intervention of the SRS War Staff from Belgrade." That's what that document says, doesn't it, and it's dated 24 October 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I cannot challenge this document, and I cannot confirm it either, but I think that it is not within the setup and function and nature of our War Staff. As for this Rankic --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did I read it correctly, that document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you read it correctly. I mean, I think that it is not in accordance with the nature of the function of the War Staff. As for this Zoran Rankic, I know that he is a man who is a craftsman, and he must have worded this clumsily. He did it just for the sake of doing it. He didn't really give any thought to serious matters. I can claim --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well let me show you another document, Exhibit P227. Now, do you see in this document, number 3, in which there are conditions for providing assistance, and number 3 is: " ... coordination with our unit command." Do you see that on this document dated 16 October 1991 from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Madam, I can confirm that Mr. Rankic did this clumsily and that this is not in accordance with the powers that he had. I claim with full responsibility that the Serb Radical Party did not have any military units of its own. Now, this Zoran Rankic, as I said, is a semi-literate person, so how he understood his role, that's his problem. And after all I know, that he did not stay on the War Staff for very long. As well as I know him, he is really a man who doesn't understand everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention now to P25, Exhibit P25. And this document is dated 9 December 1991. And it's signed by a Chetnik commander of Vukovar, Captain Slobodan Katic. And it reads: "The Chetnik commander of Vukovar, Slobodan Katic, is proposing the following warriors for promotion." And one of them listed there is Milan, do you see that one, aka Kameni, commander. Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you read it correctly, but I'm not the right person to put these questions to. I was not at the front. For example, I never met Lancuzanin. Now why they wrote all of this and what this means to them, I'm not really competent in terms of answering that kind of question. I can just confirm that we did not have such information. The Serb Radical Party did not have any units of its own. They sent persons there who were part of the setup of the Serbian army or, rather, the JNA; that is to say, when the composition of the Territorial Defence and later on within the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina, later on the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could now please see Exhibit P217, and this is order number 124, the proclamation of certain vojvodas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The interpretation was not right. This is not "naredjenje," this is "naredba." In the Serbian language, "naredba" and "naredjenje" are two completely different legal documents. "Naredjenje," "order," is a military term order, whereas "naredba," "order," is a general legal or political act, but at any rate it is at a lower level than a law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've already said this, Mr. Seselj. Witness, you are a literate man. What can you say about the term to be used in your own language? Is it a request, a motion, an order? What is it, exactly, in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Naredba" is a general act or enactment regulating a particular matter. "Naredjenje" cannot be an individual enactment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to number 3 at the bottom of -- in the B/C/S, it will be page 1. In the English, it will be page 2, to the description of Branislav Vakic, second sentence: "He participated in the liberation of Vukovar as --"

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Vakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: The name rings a bell, but I do not know about him being in Vukovar. As for this proclamation of the Chetnik vojvodas, I only watched it on television, like most citizens of Serbia who had occasion to watch this. Otherwise, I did not take part in this and I do not see any problem in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand. Am I reading the last sentence -- the second sentence correctly: "He participated in the liberation of Vukovar as commander of the Leva Supoderica volunteer unit"? And forgive my mangled pronunciation. Am I reading that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: You read it correctly, but I was never at the front-line and I don't know anything --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Ms. Biersay did not read it out right. It says "deputy commander," not "commander." Perhaps the witness was not following it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In English, the translation is "commander," and I read it as "commander."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is not the first time that you have a bad English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that. Witness, once again, you can read, you can write, you can think. As such, in the Cyrillic text, is it "deputy commander" or "commander."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: "Deputy commander," Mr. President, "deputy commander."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So "deputy commander." Very well. Witness, in 1993, some vojvodas were proclaimed. Back then, were you aware of that or was that an initiative that is solely of Mr. Seselj's account, who did not inform the members of the Serbian Radical Party of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He provided information. We knew that that was happening, but I did not take part in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You therefore knew that Mr. Seselj had appointed several vojvodas on account of their records? What is your answer? I asked you a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... for you. Did you know then that Mr. Seselj had appointed vojvodas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did know that the appointment and proclamation of them was being prepared, but I did not take part in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I was in charge of organisation and personnel. I did not have the time or was there any need for me to take part in all the activities of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj was a very -- was the highest member of the SRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, correct, he was president, but the Central Fatherland Administration was above him, and the Assembly of the Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And with respect to the Serbian Chetnik Movement, he was also at the head of that, as you described to the Trial Chamber previously; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: He was at the head, but I lost touch with the Serb Chetnik Movement when the Serb Radical Party started functioning, and I don't know anything about the Serb Chetnik Movement. I'm not even sure that it existed and functioned. You know what? When you're talking about the Serb Chetnik Movement, many people pointed out that they were Chetniks. Even our enemies --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Before discussing the Serbian Chetnik Movement, my purpose in asking you that was: In his capacity as the functionary head of these two groups, did he meet with other high-level officials from other parties?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, Dr. Vojislav Seselj met with the functionaries of other political parties only in the capacity of president of the Serb Radical Party, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And as you described in your statement, he met -- he would meet with Radovan Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, he did meet with Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did he also meet with Milan Martic, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, when I visited the Knin Krajina in the beginning of 1993, when the battle was being waged at the Medak Pocket, "Medacki Dzep," I met with all the functionaries of the Serb Krajina, but we did not have any special discussion there with regard to some particular units of the Serb Radical Party. We were interested in the position of the Serb people, whether they had food, whether they were able to engage in economic activity. We could not be involved in decision-making concerning their military operations, nor did we have any intention of doing so. We just wanted to help.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So is that a "yes," there were meetings between Mr. Seselj and Martic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know specifically of any particular meeting, but I do believe that there had been meetings. Well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And also, as you described, Mr. Seselj was also in contact with Radmilo Bogdanovic as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, with Radmilo Bogdanovic, I was in contact with him too, but these are no contacts that would lead to some special activities. Radmilo Bogdanovic was president of the Chamber of Republics, the Chamber of Republics in the Federal Assembly, and it is only natural that we were in contact, especially Dr. Seselj, who was the president of our deputies club. He was also in contact with Radoman Bozovic, who was also the president of the Chamber of Citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I may have one minute, Your Honour. And in that time, may I inquire how much time I have left, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar. Fifteen minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to the topic of the attempted kidnapping of one of your family members. When did you learn that it, in fact, was not a member of the SRS who had attempted that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I learnt that on the very same day, because my deputy in this newly-established Deputies Club, called the headquarters of the Serb Radical Party and talked about that problem. I mean, he found out that it wasn't anyone from the Serb Radical Party. And later on, we checked that again, we asked again, and we were told explicitly that Dr. Vojislav Seselj had been informed and that he condemned this kind of thing, and that it had nothing to do with the leadership of the Serb Radical Party. These are some self-styled individuals that existed at the front-line and throughout the former Yugoslavia. Many of them introduced themselves as Chetniks, and they had nothing to do with the Serb Radical Party or with the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: I'd like to turn your attention now to the encounter that you described to the Trial Chamber between you and a member of the OTP, Mr. Saxon. Now, you have a degree in law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You have been a successful politician in your own right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I don't consider myself a politician. I consider myself a patriot, and there you go, a man of letters, who writes, who is preoccupied with the fate of his people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And let me now again show you 65 ter number 7427A. That is the document that you previously recognised as being your signature, if you recall. As the Trial Chamber pointed out, the statement that you provided the OTP in 2003, you signed that statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: 2004, that's when I gave this statement, the end of May. I signed it, it wasn't read out to me, and it was Mr. Paolo Stocchi who conducted this in a very special way. He actually used my statement to the effect that I was very grateful to the Italian nation and that I see him as the nephew of the Italian officer who took me out of an Ustasha's hands when I was one year old, and in that way he prevented that Ustasha from killing me with a bayonet. And on the basis of that, he wrote up whatever he wrote up, and the last day he forced me to sign what he had written up in English. And then he said that I would be called for further interviews. And I was already fed up with those that had taken place until then. He asked me all sorts of things, "Who financed municipal committees," and at one moment I asked him whether he was asking me these questions as a CIA agent or as an investigator. He was completely going beyond the scope of the judiciary. And he said if I were to cooperate with anyone, I would cooperate with the Italian. And then this other colleague said, "Why not cooperate with the CIA when --"

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My question is simply this: And I see that you're smiling. My question is whether or not you applied your signature and initials to the pages of the 2003 statement that you gave to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: In 2003, I didn't give any statements. It was in 2004, and I did --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in on the signature of 7427A, please - it's at the bottom - to see if this perhaps refreshes your recollection of the date of that first statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you telling this Trial Chamber that although you're a man of letters and educated in the law, that you signed -- you were forced to sign this? Is that what you'd have this Trial Chamber believe?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I am telling you how it was that I was forced. As far as I can remember, and I guess I remember well, it was 2004, not 2003.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, objection. Judges, this paper here is not an integral part of the statement of Mr. Glamocanin. Have the Prosecutor show us the statement that Mr. Glamocanin did sign. What he signed here was a sheet of paper, and in his own hand he wrote out some names. This is not a signature below the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not waste any time. I've already asked questions on this topic. The Prosecution thinks it's necessary to return to the topic. I don't see the point in doing so. But have you signed, in your own language, a statement made in Serbian? Answer by "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not in Serbian, no, no way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You signed a statement in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirdly, you signed the document we see in front of us on the 30th of May, 2003?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, how could I challenge my very own signature? But I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you can see there's a signature, there is the date in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I see it, but I can't remember. I guess it's a question of age, too, if I can't remember everything. So many things have happened, I really don't know. I am familiar with all these names. We did cooperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Previously, you described to the Trial Chamber that Mr. Seselj did not talk about genocide. Did Mr. Seselj talk about the genocide of the Serbian people in his speeches?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, he did. He spoke about the genocide that took place in World War II. Well, the Ustashas killed a million Serbs during the Second World War. And there was genocidal killings of Serbs in 1991, too, in July and August, in Western Slavonia, for instance, and the area of Vukovar. There were such phenomena. They occurred in Gospic, too. And as far as our nation is concerned, it is a terrible -- it's terrible to know that the genocide of World War II is repeating itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And didn't Mr. Seselj advocate the retaliation for crimes he says were committed against Serbs in World War II?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Seselj never did that. Seselj claimed and especially stressed that we must not believe the Ustashas and pro-Ustasha forces and pro-Ustasha authorities in Croatia, just like the Serbs believed in 1941. Quite simply, our people were led to churches, incarcerated there, set alight there; they were burnt there. Then they were killed in their masses in the most atrocious ways. And they responded to the new Croatian Ustasha authorities and said, "Well, why are we to blame?" It wasn't a question of why were they to blame or not, but the fact is that they weren't to blame for anything, it's just that they were Serbs and Orthodox. And now this was repeated with the programme and all the various signs and insignia, and the intimations of new Croatian politics of the HDZ led by Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Time is of the essence. Mr. Seselj, maybe you can start your cross-examination, but the Trial Chamber has one thing to tell you beforehand. You told us, and we thank you for that, that you intend to use a book which has been published and which gave rise to confidential written submissions made by the Prosecution. If you use this book only as far as the SRS is concerned and the role played by the witness in the SRS, that's fine, but the Trial Chamber is prohibiting you from using this book in order to reveal the name of a protected witness. You have to understand that you can only use this book in order to put questions to the witness regarding the SRS, Greater Serbia, and maybe other things, but not to reveal names of witnesses. And to avoid controversies, the Trial Chamber is also asking you not to mention the title of this book, because as we already said, this is irrelevant. My fellow Judge would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to add, as far as I'm concerned, it's my opinion that I am stating here, that you are not entitled to use the excerpts of this book where you make reference to the witness we have here today, because when you wrote the book, this witness was a protected witness. So the -- so this crime of contempt is being tried by another Trial Chamber, and I believe you cannot use these excerpts for this reason.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Lattanzi, I always liked your ability to think logically, but now you have surpassed yourself and you have even put Hagel upside down, stand on his head. This statement of Mr. Glamocanin's was confidential until today. And since Mr. Glamocanin came into the courtroom and said he was testifying publicly, this is no longer confidential, and that relates to all of Mr. Glamocanin's statements. And as I respect your ability to think logically, I do, but I can't accept that. On the one hand, I respect you immensely, and on the other, I have complete resistance to that from the very insides of my being, and then you can stop me from cross-examining, if you like. But what I wanted to say is this: I informed Ms. Biersay that I was going to cross-examine only on the basis of those passages which relate to Mr. Glamocanin, and I said that was from page 68, onwards some 20 to 25 pages; but that's not essential, and she has it all. Thirdly, Judges, when two or three months ago I submitted a request to the Trial Chamber to stand up and protect Defence witnesses, I added to that at least 18 witness statements where I said that the Prosecutor was trying to seize them away from me; and they've all been translated into English, my submissions and the attachments. You rejected my submission, but you are aware of the statements. You have them in English. And now I insist that I be allowed to use all the statements which have to do with Mr. Glamocanin, and they are statements which he gave to my associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I do not know what is in your book. We did not read it. We only saw the cover page. We do not know what is in the book. It is true that this witness is no longer protected as of today, and therefore what he said or wrote is public. And I note that he has written a great number of books. He's given a great number of interviews. He's a public figure. He's a well-known person. Now, in the book you wrote, I assume you are referring to things that this person might have written or said. It might be useful to say, "Witness Glamocanin said this or that at one point in time," as long as it does not reveal the name of protected witnesses. The position of my fellow Judge is her own opinion. She is raising a legal question. She is of an opinion, and I'm of a different opinion; and since we have no jurisprudence when it comes to the Appeals Chamber regarding this, we are in the dark. In order to bypass this difficulty, if in this book there are excerpts where the witness talked about the SRS, the role you played in Vukovar, you can say, "In the book, I wrote you said this or that. Do you confirm it? Do you maintain it? Yes or no?" This is not going to jeopardise anything. What do you want to say, we'll see as we go. If the Trial Chamber believes that it is jeopardising something, we'll redact. But so far this is a very theoretical debate. I have no idea about the questions you are going to ask, so please proceed and we'll see as we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to add one thing. My problem is quite different from what Mr. Seselj and the Presiding Judge are saying. It's not the problem of confidentiality, the fact that the protective measures were granted and are no longer there and have been lifted. That's not it. The issue is that it's the book as it is, because if there are some excerpts dealing with this witness are quoted, because this witness was protected when the book was written, this will mean that it must be investigated by another Trial Chamber in order to know whether, having revealed the status of this witness at the time was correct or not, and whether this is contempt, "yes" or "no." So that's a bit of a different problem. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you understood, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Lattanzi, whether I committed contempt of court or not has nothing to do with these proceedings and the examination of this witness. Apart from the fact whether an accused can be held in contempt of court, that will have to be looked into, and then all the rest of it. But, anyway, this witness gave a statement to my associates, and he gave permission that may be disclosed to the public. When the book was published, this witness received a copy by the author of this book, and he came to speak at the public promotion of this book in the large hall of the trade union building in Belgrade. So he was there publicly. There were 3.000 people there, and he spoke about this book in public. It was a public event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if I understood you correctly, and we need your help here because we don't know what's in the book, you say this witness made written statements to your associates. There are statements, I guess that they have been certified by the competent court. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: (redacted) And you want to use this book in order to confirm statements made to your associates, but why don't you just use the statement made to the associates instead of going through the book?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I provided you with those statements directly three months ago. I haven't got them now because I threw that paper away. It's easier for me to keep it in one small book rather than having a whole pile of papers to carry around, because I have too much of that already. I don't have to rely on this at all. I'll rely on its contents, and I have almost all the contents in my head. And you're very well aware of another thing, Judges. Several months ago, when I mentioned the title of this book for the first time and when we moved into private session because of that and redacted the transcript, every subsequent time that I mentioned the book, I said, "I'm not going to say the title of the book," to avoid going into private session, so there's no need for you to caution me on that score. Now, we've only got four minutes left. Is there any sense in me starting my cross-examination with just four minutes? I was quite ready to cross-examine if I had 10 or 20 minutes, but is there really any sense in me starting when there's just four minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's best you begin your cross-examination tomorrow. The Trial Chamber will allow you to refer to the statements, but you are not to give the title of the book. I believe you agree on this. You can say, "In the statement in this book, Witness, you said this or that. Please explain." All three Judges agree on this procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you see how much I respect those decisions of yours. And when I intimated to Ms. Biersay that I would be using the book, I didn't even give the title then. I just said, "I'll use this nice book," [In English] "I'll use this beautiful book." [Interpretation] Those were my words when I informed her. I didn't want to state the title then to avoid Ms. Dahl hearing who was present there. So you see how scrupulous I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Trial Chamber is noting that your English has greatly improved, and this will help us move forward. Mr. Seselj, we will resume tomorrow at 8.30. You will have one hour, and I hope everything will run according to plan. Afterwards, Judges might have some additional questions. I don't know yet. My fellow Judge is already hinting at questions that he might have -- that he will have. Then we'll finish with this witness, and then we have another witness scheduled, 92 ter witness. So that's the programme for tomorrow. Witness, you are under oath at the moment, since you made the solemn declaration. You are not entitled to contact anyone from the OTP or to have contact with Mr. Seselj, but that would be quite difficult for you. Please avoid contacting the press also. If a reporter calls you to ask you what your impressions are so far, just tell him that you will go public later, after tomorrow, because as of now you're still in the hands of justice. And you are a lawyer, so you know exactly what I am talking about. That's it. We will meet again tomorrow at 8.30 a.m. Let's adjourn. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of December, 2008, at 8.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.15 p.m.,
